analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover routine preventive care for children without copays or deductibles.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in May 2009 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the laws governing employer plans and health insurance to require coverage of preventive care for children up to age 18, following the Bright Futures pediatric care guidelines. It would ban deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance on those services, bar insurers from penalizing doctors or dropping enrollees to dodge the requirement, and extend the same rules to individual plans. It would also keep a plan from counting as a tax-favored high-deductible plan unless it met the coverage requirement. The bill never moved after its initial referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with employer or individual health coverage would gain guaranteed no-cost pediatric preventive care — well-child visits, screenings, and immunizations under the Bright Futures guidelines — for children up to 18, without out-of-pocket charges at the point of care.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to cover 'appropriate preventive care' for each dependent child up to age 18, defined by regulation as care meeting the Bright Futures pediatric guidelines [S2][S3].
Prohibits plans from imposing deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing on those preventive services, so families would face no out-of-pocket charge at the visit [S2][S3].

Bars plans from denying or terminating enrollment, or penalizing or rewarding a child's doctor, to get around the coverage requirement, and applies the same rules to individual-market insurance [S2][S3].

Keeps a plan from being treated as a tax-favored high-deductible health plan unless it meets the pediatric preventive-care requirement, limiting the ability of high-deductible plans to sidestep it [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers sponsoring group plans would bear the cost of added covered services and of eliminating cost-sharing; much of it would be passed on through premiums. High-deductible plans would lose tax-favored status unless they complied.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers and employers sponsoring health plans

drawbacks.text: Mandating no-cost-sharing coverage raises insurers' costs, which would likely flow back to families and employers as higher premiums, spreading the cost of the sickest users of preventive care across all enrollees [S3].
The requirements would apply to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2010, giving insurers less than a year to redesign benefits and notice materials [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families with children, the benefit is concrete: pediatric checkups, screenings, and immunizations with no copay, which research links to catching problems early. The cost is real but standard for a coverage mandate — higher premiums spread across enrollees — and it would apply broadly. A fair trade-off for a targeted benefit, though a narrow bill like this duplicates what could be done in a larger health reform; indeed, comprehensive health reform enacted in 2010 imposed broader preventive-care coverage requirements without cost-sharing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2009, referred to three House committees, sent to two subcommittees, and then sat without any hearing, markup, or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Thompson (D-CA) introduced the bill on May 6, 2009, with Rep. Blumenauer, and it was referred to the Ways and Means, Education and Labor, and Energy and Commerce committees [S1][S3][S5].
The bill drew only two cosponsors, both House Democrats [S4].

In June 2009 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health and the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill never taken up, leaving it dead [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers were spared a new no-cost-sharing coverage mandate, and no one else gained — though Congress enacted broader preventive-coverage requirements in the health reform law signed in 2010, which covered much of the same ground.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and plan sponsors avoided the mandate

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and only two Democratic cosponsors, and there were no votes, so no party split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to cover pediatric preventive services with no cost-sharing and stops coverage-restriction workarounds, raising their claims costs; they would pass much of that through premiums, so families both gain the benefit and share the cost. The bill's coverage and cost-sharing provisions were later enacted more broadly in the 2010 health reform law.
Plan sponsors would bear higher benefit costs, partly offset by healthier workforces and the ability to negotiate provider reimbursement rates under the bill's savings clause.

industries.industry: High-deductible plans and health savings account ecosystem
industries.note: By conditioning high-deductible plan status on meeting the pediatric preventive-care requirement, the bill constrains how high-deductible plans could structure benefits without losing tax-favored treatment.
Guaranteed no-cost-sharing coverage of guideline-based well-child care means more patient visits and fewer insurer penalties for following the Bright Futures guidelines.
